notable_claims: SWITCH is accused of manipulating public information by blocking specific newsgroups and packets to local eunet chapters.
The University of Cincinnati moved to terminate accounts for users telnetting to 'game' and IRC hosts.
Arguments are made that familiarity with network resources, including recreational use, is a valuable professional skill for programmers.
classification.summary: This digest summarizes debates regarding network censorship and acceptable use policies in academic environments. Key discussions focus on SWITCH's filtering of Usenet newsgroups and packets in Switzerland, as well as the University of Cincinnati's policy of terminating accounts for users accessing IRC and game hosts via telnet.
classification.title: Abstract of CAF-News 02.12

notable_claims: Private organizations acting as information providers for universities can commit censorship.
SWITCH allegedly used false claims about Swiss law to justify banning newsgroups and discourage secondary feeds.
classification.summary: Jurgen Botz argues against Brad Templeton's claim that a private entity cannot commit censorship. Botz contends that SWITCH, as an information provider for higher education institutions, has a moral responsibility to avoid manipulating information flow. He specifically criticizes SWITCH for claiming banned newsgroups were against Swiss law to discourage member institutions from using secondary feeds.
classification.title: Re: Censorship and bigotry come up strong in Switzerland

identity.subject: Article 1--Re: Censorship and bigotry come up strong in Switzerland

notable_claims: Censorship is defined as the use or threat of violence to control information flow.
Only governments can legally perform censorship in the strict sense.
The right not to be forced to publish or transmit information is a key component of freedom of expression.
classification.summary: Brad Templeton engages in a debate regarding the definition of censorship in the context of academic and network environments. He argues that true censorship requires the use or threat of force/violence, typically wielded by governments, rather than administrative decisions by universities or network providers. The discussion specifically references actions planned by SWITCH.
classification.title: Re: Censorship and bigotry come up strong in Switzerland

identity.subject: Article 2--Re: Censorship and bigotry come up strong in Switzerland

notable_claims: Usenet is not a public utility or a legal right, but depends on the owners of the hardware.
SWITCH removed various newsgroups without prior notice via administrative fiat.
SWITCH previously blocked port 25 (SMTP) to favor X.400 software testing.
SWITCH was blocking NNTP, Telnet, and FTP traffic to local EUnet/CHUUG sites.
organizations: Swiss Federal Institute of Technology in Lausanne
classification.summary: Mitchell Wyle discusses the restriction of Usenet newsgroups and network protocols by SWITCH in Switzerland. The post includes a lengthy quote from Chip Salzenberg arguing that Usenet is not a public utility or a right, but subject to the property rights of machine owners. Wyle provides technical evidence of SWITCH blocking specific ports (NNTP, Telnet, FTP) to local EUnet sites.
classification.title: Censorship and bigotry come up strong in Switzerland

identity.subject: Article 3--Re: Censorship and bigotry come up strong in Switzerland

notable_claims: Censorship is defined as the act of an official prohibiting things, rather than a private group choosing not to provide something.
The decision by a USENET feed to exclude specific newsgroups is not censorship.
classification.summary: John Stanley argues against the broad application of the term 'censorship' to describe the actions of private entities or funding bodies. He specifically contends that a USENET feed choosing not to carry certain newsgroups does not constitute censorship, as users remain free to seek alternative feeds.
classification.title: Article 4--Re: Censorship and bigotry come up strong in Switzerland

identity.subject: Article 4--Re: Censorship and bigotry come up strong in Switzerland

notable_claims: SWITCH is not a private company and follows governmental requests.
SWITCH proposed allowing newsgroups if the requesting University takes responsibility for them.
Governmental filtering of legal newsgroups may allow the state to promote or suppress specific information.
classification.summary: Guy Genilloud discusses the role of SWITCH in managing newsgroup access in Switzerland. He argues that because SWITCH is influenced by governmental organizations, its ability to filter legal newsgroups constitutes a form of censorship. He questions whether universities should be forced to take 'responsibility' for requested newsgroups as a condition for access.

notable_claims: Student inaction regarding service shutdowns is often due to a belief that petitions will not effect change.
Administrators should open policy meetings and seek user input rather than acting arbitrarily.
classification.summary: Sean Casey responds to Mark Hittinger regarding the shutdown of controversial network services. Casey argues that a lack of student petitions does not imply a lack of seriousness, but rather a systemic distrust of authority. He suggests that administrators should proactively involve users in policy-making instead of acting arbitrarily.
classification.title: Article 6--Re: Why I hate IRC

notable_claims: System administrators at the University of Cincinnati were killing accounts for connecting to IRC, MUDs, and certain foreign hosts.
Access to Unix systems was restricted to specific classes (mainly Computer Science) at some universities.
classification.summary: A discussion regarding the censorship of telnet connections and account terminations at the University of Cincinnati for accessing IRC or MUDs. John Schultz argues against blanket bans on external connections, citing his use of a guest account at MIT/FSF to gain Unix experience unavailable to non-CS students at his own institution.
classification.title: Re: Telnet Censorship

notable_claims: Recreational network use (IRC, MUDs) serves as a source of information and professional networking.
Familiarity with Linux can save institutions money by repurposing existing equipment instead of buying new workstations.
Proficiency with network resources is a desirable trait for hiring programmers.
classification.summary: Lawrence C. Foard responds to a claim that gaming on academic computers should be banned due to resource scarcity. He argues that recreational use of the network, including IRC and MUDs, provides professional value and technical skills. He further suggests that familiarity with open-source tools like Linux can reduce institutional costs.
classification.title: Article 8--Re: Telnet Censorship

notable_claims: Computer policies must be consistent with a university's Student Code to protect freedom of expression and due process.
Federal courts have consistently struck down speech restrictions at public universities.
Due process is required before serious punishments can be applied to students for computer infractions.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie responds to a discussion on IRC abuse by arguing that network discipline must be governed by published policies and university judicial procedures. He provides an FAQ and references to the Electronic Frontier Foundation's (EFF) archives regarding computer policy, academic freedom, and relevant case law. The post emphasizes the necessity of due process and user participation in policy development.
